summary:
Visitors to Indiana stand under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and now issues passports only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged under the code 'SWS25' and an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth potentially treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a separate exposure: secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can disclose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

Indiana's identity documents are the sharpest state-level constraint. The Bureau of Motor Vehicles' ban on gender-marker changes to driver's licences and identification cards took effect on 1 February 2026, ending the long-standing route by which a resident could obtain such a change through a court-ordered gender change or a physician statement. The ban culminated an administrative rule change the Bureau initiated; LGBTQ advocates who testified warned that it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents.

Birth-certificate marker changes were already closed by the courts. In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined, in split votes, to hear two cases brought by transgender girls seeking to change the gender on their birth certificates, leaving appeals-court rulings standing that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the General Assembly codifies them. One of the cases involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access.

Facility use is the second active front. On 27 January 2026 the Indiana Senate approved Senate Bill 182 by a 37-8 party-line vote and sent it to the House. The bill would require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity. It would also create statutory definitions for sex and gender, ban amendments to birth certificates, and restrict housing in prisons. Author Senator Liz Brown, a Republican from Fort Wayne, said the proposal lets women continue to have their private spaces; opponents including GenderNexus argued that allowing anyone directly or indirectly injured to sue a school over an alleged violation would encourage harassment-style enforcement.

Independent legal-risk assessments place Indiana near the top of the national range. Erin in the Morning's February 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map grades anti-trans legal risk state by state and states that Indiana's 2026 identification policy now places it among the harshest anti-trans states in the country, with bathroom-ban escalation driving its adult-risk rating; the July 2026 assessment records the same trajectory.
tangentialFactors:
Indiana's restrictions sit inside a wider national pattern. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances; twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is documented: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol and was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identification rules vary sharply by state. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, and rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
localsOnly:
Indiana residents can no longer change the gender marker on a driver's licence or state identification card. The Bureau of Motor Vehicles' ban took effect on 1 February 2026 and removed both the court-ordered gender change route and the physician-statement route that had been available, following an administrative rule change initiated by the Bureau itself. Advocates who testified against the change warned that residents who have not updated their documents will be outed whenever they present them.

Birth certificates are separately closed to marker changes. The May 2023 Indiana Supreme Court denials left in place appeals-court rulings that trial courts have no authority to order gender-marker changes on birth certificates unless the General Assembly legislates them, so no judicial route exists at present.

Senate Bill 182, approved 37-8 by the Senate on 27 January 2026 and pending in the House, would go further than facilities. It would write statutory definitions of sex and gender into Indiana law, bar amendments to birth certificates, restrict housing assignments in prisons, and require public K-12 schools and state universities to assign multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas by reproductive biology at birth. Its private right of action lets anyone directly or indirectly injured sue a school over an alleged violation, a provision GenderNexus argued would invite harassment-style enforcement.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Senate Bill 182 has been enacted, amended or stalled in the Indiana House is unresolved in the sources; only the 27 January 2026 Senate passage is documented.

Whether Indiana currently operates a statewide facility restriction applying to adults outside schools, or a criminal penalty for trans facility use, is not sourced here. The sources document the school and university provisions of a pending bill and the general national count of states with such bans, not Indiana's own adult-facing position.

No source in this inventory records an enforcement action, arrest or prosecution under any Indiana restriction affecting trans people, so the practical enforcement picture for the state is unresolved.

Whether Indiana has issued its own travel guidance for trans visitors, or whether any foreign government has singled Indiana out in an advisory, is not sourced.

The precise scope of the Bureau of Motor Vehicles rule, including whether it affects identification cards already issued with a changed marker, is not stated in the sources.
